title: On over-fitting in model selection and subsequent selection bias in performance evaluation
harvard_reference: Cawley, G.C. and Talbot, N.L.C. (2010) 'On over-fitting in model selection and subsequent selection bias in performance evaluation', Journal of Machine Learning Research, 11(70), pp. 2079-2107. Available at: https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html (Accessed: 27 September 2026).
abstract_summary: The paper examines model selection (hyperparameter tuning) driven by numerical optimisation of a criterion such as k-fold cross-validation. Decomposing the criterion's error into bias and variance, the authors argue that low variance matters at least as much as unbiasedness, because a non-negligible variance lets the hyperparameters over-fit the selection criterion just as parameters can over-fit the training data. Empirically, this over-fitting in model selection degrades generalisation by amounts comparable to the differences between competing learning algorithms. A second contribution shows that several common performance-evaluation protocols are susceptible to a selection bias arising from this over-fitting and are therefore unreliable, and the paper describes protocols that avoid the bias (treating model selection as an integral part of model fitting, performed independently inside each resampling fold). Although the study focuses on cross-validation, the authors state the conclusions apply to any model-selection practice that optimises a criterion over a finite sample, including Bayesian evidence and performance bounds.

claims_supported.claim: Selecting hyperparameters and estimating performance on the same cross-validation folds produces optimistically biased estimates; nested cross-validation avoids this selection bias.
claims_supported.where: Section 1 (p. 2080): the paper names 'the undesirable optimistic bias that can arise due to over-fitting in model selection' and states that unbiased performance evaluation is likely to require protocols 'such a nested cross-validation or double cross (Stone, 1974)'. Section 5 introduction (p. 2094): avoiding the bias requires treating training and model selection together as integral parts of model fitting, never performed separately during evaluation. Section 5.1 (p. 2095): the unbiased 'internal' protocol performs model selection independently within each fold of the resampling procedure, i.e. nested CV. Section 5.3 (pp. 2102-2103) and Table 8: when hyperparameters are tuned on the whole design set and the same data are then re-partitioned for cross-validated testing ('external' protocol), the test data are no longer statistically pure and 'we should therefore expect to observe an optimistic bias'; Table 8 shows the external protocol exhibits 'a consistently optimistic bias' relative to the internal (nested) protocol on all thirteen benchmarks, statistically significant on eleven, and the authors conclude it 'should not be used in practice'. Section 6 Conclusions (p. 2103): model selection 'should be conducted independently in each trial in order to prevent selection bias'.

Claim 1 was verified against the full text of the JMLR PDF (29 pages; sections 1, 5, 5.1, 5.3, 6 and Table 8), not only the abstract.
caveats: The abstract itself does not use the phrase 'nested cross-validation' or 'optimistic bias'; those appear in the body. The paper's own terminology for the recommended protocol is the 'internal' cross-validation protocol (model selection repeated inside each fold), which it equates with nested cross-validation / 'double cross' in the introduction. The biased 'external' protocol studied in Section 5.3 tunes hyperparameters once on the entire data set before the same data are cross-validated, which is the leakage the claim describes; the paper does not literally use the wording 'same cross-validation folds', so the report should paraphrase rather than quote. The issue number 70 is JMLR's retrospective paper number shown on the article page; many citation styles cite JMLR papers by volume only (11), which is also acceptable.
